This page collects the questions that come up most often when getting
started with EpiSODIC - about data, running it day to day, and
accounts. If your question isn't here, the README's "Data format" and
"Environment variables" sections and the "Architecture overview",
"Deployment", and "Detection and reconciliation" vignettes go deeper on
most of these topics; and if it still isn't answered anywhere, that's
worth telling us, since it means this page is missing something it
should cover.

## How do I prepare my data?

Don't worry about getting this perfect by hand - that's exactly what
`episodic_check_cases()` is for. Hand it your extract, however rough:

```r
EpiSODIC::episodic_check_cases(my_cases)
```

No database, no configuration, nothing changed - it just reads your data
and tells you, in one pass, everything it finds: which column is wrong,
how many rows are affected, which rows those are, what the offending
values look like, and what to do about each. It also separates two kinds
of finding, so you're never left guessing which ones actually block you:
**problems** (a run refuses to start until these are fixed - a date that
doesn't parse, a value outside the allowed set) and **advice** (a run
proceeds regardless, but it's worth a look - one pathogen spelled two
ways, no `ward` on any hospital row). Run it, fix what it flags as a
problem, run it again - most people get to a clean report in two or
three passes. The README's "Data format" section has the full column
contract this is checking against, including the exact allowed values
for `care_line`, `institution_type`, and `sex`.

## Do I need to send all of my positives each day, or only the latest results?

Send everything, every time - don't try to filter to "what's new" on
your end. That's not extra work you're doing for nothing: **deduplication
is EpiSODIC's job, not yours**. Every row needs a `source_key` that's
unique within your own source system; re-sending a row EpiSODIC has
already seen (same `source_key`) is simply a no-op, so a full daily
export is always safe to resend, and there's no bookkeeping on your side
to track what's already been sent. Isolates from the same patient and
pathogen are then collapsed into one case per episode automatically,
using the episode length configured per pathogen. If you instead try to
send only "new" results, you risk EpiSODIC quietly missing a positive
that your own filtering logic mis-classified as already sent - so the
simpler approach is also the safer one. The one thing this feed should
never include is negative results; it's deliberately positives-only.

## What do I do when a lab result was rectified or corrected, but EpiSODIC already has the now-false positive?

First: don't worry, this happens, and it's a normal part of running any
detection system on live laboratory data - it isn't something you did
wrong. EpiSODIC doesn't offer a way to delete or edit an individual case
once it's been loaded, and that's deliberate: the case data is the
audit trail every dossier and every report is built from, so quietly
removing a row would make past results harder to explain rather than
easier. What this means in practice depends on where the correction
lands:

- **If the correction arrives before a cluster was raised from it** (or
  before the affected run), you don't need to do anything - it simply
  won't be part of any signal, since it's just data sitting in the
  database like any other case.
- **If a cluster has already been raised (or affected) because of it**,
  handle it the same way you'd handle any signal that turns out not to
  reflect reality: assess and close it in the dashboard with the
  classification that fits (e.g. not an outbreak), noting the correction
  in the assessment. That decision - including the reasoning - becomes
  part of the cluster's own audit trail, which is exactly the record you
  want to be able to point to later if anyone asks why a signal didn't
  lead anywhere.
- **If a stream is regularly noisy for a reason like this** (a lab or
  feed that corrects unusually often), muting it for a defined period is
  the right tool, with the reason recorded - see the mute action on a
  cluster's dossier.

If this is happening often enough that it's a recurring nuisance rather
than an occasional correction, that's worth raising with whoever owns
your extract/transform step - the earlier a correction happens before
data reaches EpiSODIC, the less cleanup it costs anyone downstream.

## How do I create a new account?

There's no self-service sign-up screen, and that's by design - only
whoever administers your instance's database provisions accounts, which
keeps sign-in tied to real board membership rather than being
open-ended. If that's you, it's one function call:

```r
Sys.setenv(EPISODIC_DB = "/path/to/episodic.sqlite")  # or your MariaDB/MySQL DSN

EpiSODIC::episodic_provision_user(
  username = "jdoe", full_name = "Jane Doe", email = "j.doe@example.org",
  password = "a-temporary-password"
)
```

Pick any temporary password you like - the account is created with a
forced password change, so the new holder is required to set their own
private password the very first time they sign in, and the temporary
one you typed never lingers as their real credential. Pass
`role = "admin"` instead of the default `"assessor"` for someone who
also needs dossier reconciliation and archiving privileges, beyond
recording assessments. If someone forgets their password or needs their
access removed, that's also a job for whoever administers the database
(there's no self-service reset either) - reach out to them rather than
trying to work around it yourself.

## Must I run this on my own machine, or must I host it somewhere?

Either is genuinely fine - EpiSODIC doesn't assume one or the other, and
plenty of setups do each:

- **On your own machine**: `episodic_run_app()` opens the dashboard
  locally, and you (or a scheduled task on that same machine) run
  `episodic_run_cron()` on whatever cadence suits you. This is the
  simplest way to get started, and exactly what `episodic_demo()` does
  under the hood.
- **Hosted somewhere shared**: a server running `episodic_run_app()`
  behind your organisation's usual access setup, with `episodic_run_cron()`
  scheduled separately (cron, a Windows scheduled task, a CI pipeline -
  there's nothing EpiSODIC-specific about the scheduling mechanism
  itself). This is the natural choice once more than one person needs to
  reach the dashboard, since read access is anonymous to anyone who can
  reach the app - only classifying a cluster requires signing in.

Both point at the same kind of database (a local SQLite file, or a
shared MariaDB/MySQL server via `EPISODIC_DB`), so you're not locked
into your first choice - moving from "trying it out on my laptop" to "a
shared instance the whole board uses" is a deployment change, not a
data or code change. See the "Deployment" vignette for the full walk-through.

## More questions worth answering here

The five above are the ones every new user runs into first. Here are
ten more that come up quickly after that - happy to keep expanding this
page as more surface:

1. How do I know whether a scheduled `episodic_run_cron()` run actually
   succeeded, partially loaded, or failed outright - without digging
   through logs?
2. Can I try EpiSODIC out against a throwaway database first, before
   pointing it at anything real?
3. What happens to detection if I don't have postcode, ward, or
   institution-activity data for some (or all) of my cases - do I lose
   the whole picture, or just parts of it?
4. How do I change the dashboard and report language for my instance?
5. What's the difference between an `assessor` and an `admin` account,
   and how do I decide who needs which?
6. How do I tune detection thresholds (or priority score weights) for my
   own organisation without forking the package?
7. Can more than one board member review and classify the same cluster,
   and what happens if they'd disagree?
8. I have more than one laboratory system or data source - can I combine
   them into a single EpiSODIC feed?
9. Is patient-identifying information ever shown in the dashboard or in
   outbreak reports sent to clinical colleagues?
10. My organisation isn't in the Netherlands - does the geography panel
    (the choropleth map) still work for us?
